title: When Systems Are Running but Payments Are Not Moving
summary:
The IT systems processing a payment can show a green light while a customer’s payment is going nowhere. The servers are running, there is enough processing capacity and no application has reported an outage. Yet somewhere along the journey, a transaction is waiting in a queue.
For a bank monitoring individual systems, everything may appear healthy. The customer is still waiting for their money.
 At Sibos this year, I discussed what this gap means for banks and their customers. It raises a question for financial institutions: how much does knowing that the infrastructure is working tell us about the service being delivered?
Understanding the Layers of the Payment Journey
Understanding that gap starts with the layers a payment passes through, from older mainframes to middleware and newer applications.
Silo-based IT monitoring tells the bank about each system’s condition, but does not necessarily reveal what happens between them. A transaction may require manual intervention from someone who is absent, or a queue may be moving more slowly than expected. Neither situation requires a system to go down.
Business activity monitoring follows the customer journey from beginning to end. It establishes what normal behaviour looks like across successive stages and identifies departures that need investigation.
Context matters here. The first Monday of the month, after salaries have been paid, can look different from the third. Retail payments and remittances have their own patterns too. Understanding these differences helps teams recognise unusual delays without treating every variation as a problem.
Customers Expect an Answer While They Wait
That understanding of the payment journey also helps banks answer a basic customer question: where is my payment? 
With instant payments, the genie is out of the bottle. Customers are accustomed to ordering something and tracking it to their front door, often with an estimated delivery time. They increasingly expect comparable visibility from their financial institution.
One customer example shows how different the experience can be within the same banking group. Following a merger, the bank had two operating centres with separate data environments. In the centre using Vyntra’s solution, a customer service employee could look up a transaction and answer a caller in around 30 seconds. 
For an enquiry involving the other centre, the answer could take three days. The front office had to contact operations, which might then need IT to retrieve archived information. The result travelled back through the same chain and almost four hours of staff time could be involved.
Giving customer service direct access to transaction information reduces the internal work required to answer a routine question. It also means customers can receive an answer during their call.
Detecting Delays Before Customers Report Them
Answering an enquiry quickly matters, but the same visibility can help a bank identify a delay before the customer calls. This becomes particularly important when a payment holds up the business activity it was intended to support.
In a trade finance example I discussed at Sibos, a container ship could not leave because a required payment had become blocked along the transaction chain. The captain contacted the corporate customer, which then contacted the bank. The customer’s complaint was the bank’s first indication of the problem.
This illustrates why the timing of detection matters. A payment delay can interrupt commercial activity even when the systems processing it remain available.
Real-time visibility gives operations teams an opportunity to investigate an abnormal flow earlier. It cannot guarantee that every disruption will be avoided, but it gives the bank a chance to respond before the customer has to report it.
A Passport for Each Transaction
Investigating a delayed payment also means understanding what has happened along its journey, including which checks it has passed through. We describe the record of those checks as collecting ‘Know Your Transaction’ passport stamps.
When a transaction passes through sanctions screening, its record captures the check, the result and the time. Other controls, including anti-money laundering and fraud checks, contribute their own stamps.
If the transaction reaches a stage without an expected stamp, the missing record can trigger an alert. Teams can investigate the gap and retrieve the history when asked how a payment was processed.
Integrity checks add another dimension by detecting changes to the account number, amount, currency or beneficiary. A change does not automatically mean wrongdoing. There may be a valid explanation, but the institution needs to detect and record it.
This brings together the transaction’s status, the checks it has passed through and any changes made along the way. It provides a single version of the truth that customer service, operations and compliance teams can use.
Making Transaction Intelligence easier to access
Once that transaction history is available in one place, the next question is how easily people can use it. A natural-language interface could allow customers and internal teams to ask questions without needing to understand technical transaction fields.
A corporate customer could, for example, ask how their payment activity across two countries has changed over the past three months. The underlying transaction data would supply the answer, with a language model presenting it in an accessible form and allowing follow-up questions. Audit and compliance teams could use the same approach to query the transaction history.
The value depends on the information behind the interface. Banks need a connected record of where a payment is, which checks it has passed through and what has changed along the way. Making that record accessible helps people answer questions and investigate problems using the same information.

Improved visibility helps customer service answer enquiries quickly and allows operations to detect delays before complaints arise. Maintaining a complete record of checks, or transaction passports, ensures transparency across customer service, operations, and compliance teams.

title: UK Businesses Back Greener Banking, but Economic Climate Risks Undermining Support
summary:
Ahead of COP31, UK businesses are the most confident in Europe about Britain’s sustainable finance credentials, but most say affordability and growth must come first during uncertain economic times.
More than half of UK business decision-makers (‘businesses’) (52%) believe their country is a global leader in sustainable finance, ahead of every other European market surveyed, according to new research from CRIF. 
That confidence is potentially translating into greater support for greener, more sustainable financial providers, with 57% saying they are more likely to choose a financial provider that demonstrates strong ESG practices.
For businesses, a sustainable provider is about both how it operates, such as tracking its emissions and what it invests in, and what it offers customers, from green loans and finance for electric vehicles and solar panels to insurance for low-carbon projects.
However, the current challenging economic climate is testing this support. Six in ten (63%) say affordability of products and services must take priority over sustainability commitments in times of uncertainty, while more than half (56%) say banks, insurers and financial providers should prioritise supporting economic growth, even if this slows ESG progress.
The findings reflect the wider pressures on businesses’ green ambitions. Two-thirds of UK organisations (66%) cite high costs as a barrier to reaching net zero, according to the UK Net Zero Business Census 2025. 
Sara Costantini, Regional Director, UK & Ireland at CRIF, said: “UK leaders can head into COP31 buoyed by the fact that UK businesses are the most confident in Europe about their country’s performance in sustainable finance, with many favouring providers with strong ESG credentials.
“But this support is fragile. With ongoing economic uncertainty, affordability comes first for most businesses, and there is a risk that environmental priorities slip down the agenda just as COP31 puts the focus on turning commitments into investment.
“Green products often involve additional assessment, classification and reporting, which can add costs for providers and their customers. Maintaining ESG commitments during tough economic times is critical and providers that use better data and analytics to price and reward progress can make sure that sustainability and affordability don’t become an either/or choice.”
The findings come ahead of COP31 in Antalya, where leaders have put turning climate commitments into investment at the centre of the agenda.
CRIF supports banks, insurers and businesses to measure and evidence sustainability through its ESG services. CRIF’s ESG Analytics helps providers assess the ESG performance of the companies and customers they work with, while Synesgy enables businesses to evaluate the sustainability credentials of their entire supply chain.
The research forms part of CRIF’s Banking on Banks 2026 series. The first report, launched in June, looks at the biggest financial pressures currently facing European consumers and businesses. The second report, published in October, looks at the financial services gap between consumers and businesses.

title: The Rise of the ‘Intentional Shopper’ – Cost of Living Reshapes Spending Habits and Priorities
summary:
The cost-of-living crisis is leaving a lasting mark on the way people shop, with new data from Clearpay revealing a shift towards intentional spending, as Brits prioritise value, transparency and control over impulse purchasing and traditional rewards.
More than half (53%) of consumers say going through a period when money was tight has shaped how they think about money. That experience is translating into more considered purchasing behaviour as 85% of consumers now tend to wait or compare options before committing to a purchase. A further four in five (80%) would rather abandon a purchase altogether than compromise on quality or value. 
The findings suggest that while consumers remain willing to spend, they are becoming much more selective about where their money goes and how they make payments. Almost nine in 10 (89%) say transparency in cost matters more than rewards when choosing how to pay, while 90% prefer transparent upfront costs over rewards or perks. 
As consumers become more deliberate about spending, offering clarity around the total cost and choice over how to pay is increasingly important. Having payment options at checkout is a priority, with more than nine in 10 (92%) Brits saying they feel more in control when they can choose how and when they pay. Similarly, 90% say they are more likely to complete a purchase when their preferred payment method is available.
Technology is reinforcing this considered approach to shopping. Almost half (46%) of consumers have already used AI to research products or compare shopping options. AI is currently playing its biggest role before shoppers reach the checkout, as nearly a third (30%) have used it to find the best price or deal, 27% to research and compare products and 25% to check reviews. 
Rich Bayer, CEO at Clearpay, said: “The last few years have changed how people shop. Consumers haven’t stopped spending, but they are thinking harder about what represents genuine value and they want payment methods that suit their needs. They are much less willing to accept hidden costs, poor-quality purchases or payment options that leave them uncertain about what they will ultimately pay.
“For retailers, this means the traditional levers of discounts, points and perks will only go so far. Increasingly, the businesses that win people over will be those that make it easy to compare, understand the cost and stay in control. As technology gives shoppers even more information before they buy, transparency at the checkout is only going to become more important.”

title: RTGS.global Adds AMINA Bank to Its Cross-Border Payment Network, Bridging Fiat and Digital Asset Banking
summary:
RTGS.global and AMINA Bank AG (AMINA) have today announced a partnership that adds regulated digital asset banking capabilities to RTGS.global’s cross-border payment network. The partnership gives eligible RTGS.global clients access to AMINA’s FINMA-regulated banking services, making it easier for businesses and financial institutions operating across traditional and digital assets to access banking services and move money across borders. To start, services spanning fiat accounts in CHF and EUR  with local payment rails alongside digital wallets are available through a single platform. USD and GBP fiat accounts will be added in due course.
AMINA is the first bank on the RTGS.global network to offer both fiat and digital asset services. Eligible RTGS.global clients who onboard with AMINA will hold accounts directly in their own business name and can manage those accounts through RTGS.global’s platform alongside their other banking relationships.
Payment service providers and money transfer operators increasingly need banking partners that handle fiat accounts, local payment rails, and digital asset wallets under one platform rather than sourcing each capability separately.
“When clients are operating across traditional and digital assets, they need banking and payment infrastructure that works across the full journey, rather than having to piece together different providers for different markets,” said Felipe Hillard, Chief Commercial Officer at RTGS.global. “Amina brings established banking and digital asset capabilities into the RTGS.global network, giving clients more options across currencies while making it simpler to move money across borders.”
“Fiat banking and digital asset services have largely developed as separate worlds, and businesses moving money cross-border are the ones paying the cost of that divide,” said Myles Harrison, Chief Product Officer at AMINA. “AMINA joined the RTGS.global network because it connects us directly with those businesses looking for a banking partner that can work across both.”
The partnership will initially focus on multi-currency accounts, payment capabilities and digital asset wallets. The two organisations plan to explore further collaboration as the relationship develops, including potential opportunities for AMINA to participate as an FX pricing participant on the RTGS.global platform.

title: Fourthline and Veridas Complete Merger to Create a European Leader in Bank-Grade Digital Identity
summary:
Fourthline and Veridas today announce the completion of their merger, first announced on 16 July 2026. The transaction closed on 3 November 2026 following the satisfaction of all closing conditions.  
 
The funding will be used to accelerate product innovation, pursue strategic M&A, refinance debt, and support a shareholding reorganization that includes partial liquidity for Veridas shareholders. Both businesses will be EBITDA-positive at close. The combination is expected to deliver €20m in annual run-rate synergies. With limited customer overlap and complementary markets, most of that growth will come from offering each company's proprietary technology underpinning the full scope of IDV products to the other's customers. 
 
Leadership and governance 
 
Fourthline CEO, Paul Stoddart, will lead the combined entity as Chief Executive Officer. Finch Capital Managing Partner, Radboud Vlaar will chair the Supervisory Board. Eduardo Azanza, Veridas CEO, will become President of the combined company. ​Esteban Morrás, until now president of Veridas, ​Finch Capital’s Philip van Engers, and Alfonso Diaz, Investment Director at Seaya Andromeda, will join the Fourthline Group Holding B.V. Supervisory Board. Headquarters of the combined company will be in Amsterdam, with offices in Stockholm, Pamplona, Barcelona, Mexico, São Paulo & Boston. 
 
What customers gain 
 
Fourthline and Veridas have joined forces to create a global bank-grade identity platform: sovereign AI, modular compliance, and proprietary anti-fraud and biometric technology across Europe, Latin America, and the US. One trusted partner for end-to-end KYC, AML, and Identity compliance. From today, customers of either company can work with one provider across Europe, Latin America, Mexico and the US. Both platforms continue to run with full continuity of service, existing contracts, integrations, and local support. Integration will follow in phases, and customers do not need to take any action. 
 
Why the combination matters now 
 
Regulated businesses face two pressures at once: fraud is increasingly AI-generated, including deepfake and synthetic-identity attacks, and the compliance perimeter is widening following the EU AMLR, MiCA, eIDAS 2.0 and national age-verification legislation, CNBV & CUB in Latin America and Mexico. Global spend on digital identity verification is expected to reach nearly $19 billion in 2026 and grow by 55% to more than $29 billion by 2030, according to Juniper Research. 
 
The same research finds biometric verification is the fastest-growing modality and that “enterprise buyers are consolidating spend with providers that cover the full identity lifecycle across markets and regulations.” 
 
The combined company addresses both, bringing together Fourthline's compliance and decisioning, built for regulated financial services providers in Northern and Central Europe, and Veridas's biometric, document and voice technology, deployed across Southern Europe, Latin America and the US. The stack is fully proprietary. Qualified Trust Services are delivered by Fourthline Trust Services, a QTSP. The result: regulated businesses can grow into new markets with confidence.

title: Trading 212 Partners With Cardamon to Enhance Regulatory Compliance Across All Products and Markets
summary:
Trading 212 has partnered with London-based regtech firm, Cardamon, to deploy its AI compliance platform across multiple jurisdictions, markets and products in which it operates.
Cardamon’s AI platform enables regulated financial services businesses like Trading 212 to enter new markets and launch new products while staying compliant. Acting as a set of digital teammates working for a client’s compliance team, Cardamon’s technology maps a firm’s unique regulatory position in a way that is up to 20x faster than legacy compliance platforms or internal manual processes.
Within the first few weeks of implementation, Trading 212 reported a significant reduction in the time its compliance team spent on certain regulatory monitoring and mapping workflows.
Rather than operating as a standalone compliance tool, Cardamon integrates directly into Trading 212's existing systems and workflows, including Slack and Jira. Its AI agents can identify relevant regulatory changes, notify the appropriate teams and create tasks within the tools they already use. This allows Trading 212 to embed regulatory compliance into its day-to-day operations, without adding another layer of systems or processes for its teams to manage.
Areg Nzsdejan, Co-Founder & CEO of Cardamon: "Trading 212 is a great example of how Cardamon can help financial institutions manage regulatory complexity as they grow. When you're expanding rapidly across multiple markets, jurisdictions and products, the regulatory complexity grows with you. Traditional compliance processes can struggle to keep up, particularly when teams are managing different requirements across different systems.
"What makes Cardamon different is that it understands a firm's specific regulatory requirements and works directly within its existing operations. It can identify the regulatory changes that matter, assess their impact and help teams take action, all within the tools they already use. For a business operating at Trading 212's scale, that means less time spent navigating compliance processes and more capacity to support continued growth."
Once embedded, Cardamon’s AI agents can map a new client’s regulatory position in minutes - rather than the customary months - allowing the platform to become truly customised and relevant to that client’s unique set of requirements from the outset. This horizon scanning is a dynamic, constant process too. Rather than relying on periodic gap analysis, Cardamon provides Trading 212 with a real-time collaborative view of its regulatory position in every jurisdiction that matters and in whichever language the reviewer needs.
A business as large as Trading 212 will receive many regulatory updates every day. Cardamon ensures that Trading 212 only sees the updates that matter to Trading 212’s individual business, jurisdictions and product lines. 
Alexandra Meres, Group Regulatory and Policy Lead at Trading 212: "Trading 212 has grown rapidly, both in scale and in the range of products and markets we serve. That growth brings greater regulatory responsibility and complexity. What's particularly valuable about Cardamon is that it helps us manage this complexity by fitting directly into the systems and workflows our teams already use. We're not having to build new processes around another piece of technology. Instead, we're making our existing operations more efficient and giving our teams the tools they need to stay on top of regulatory change as the business continues to grow."
The platform then tells clients what impact a relevant update will have on their business and recommends what needs to be done about it. This impact assessment is delivered by Cardamon using clients’ own methodology, ensuring that what clients receive is totally tailored to their own specific set of requirements. Cardamon’s agentic capability also means that it can go beyond alerting clients to regulatory updates or change. If instructed, Cardamon’s agents will update policies and controls, and put in place the necessary regulatory changes. This reduces rather than adds to a compliance team’s workload and allows Cardamon to provide end-to-end support for the compliance workflow. 
Cardamon is a graduate of Y Combinator 2025. Trading 212 joins a long list of market leading firms using Cardamon to simplify compliance in a fast-moving, high-stakes industry including Nubank and Paddle.
